name: Second Branchial Cleft Anomaly

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiologic Diagnostic Criteria for Branchial Cleft Anomalies

criteria.description: Presence of a painless, fluctuant lateral neck mass located anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Identification of an external opening or sinus tract along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Ultrasound, CT, or MRI demonstrating a well-circumscribed cystic lesion in the lateral neck consistent with branchial cleft origin
Histological confirmation showing cyst lined by squamous or respiratory epithelium with lymphoid tissue in the wall

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of a characteristic lateral neck cystic mass with supportive imaging findings; histopathology if excised
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by imaging; histopathology confirms diagnosis post-excision.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Painless, fluctuant lateral neck cystic mass anterior to sternocleidomastoid
searchTerms: soft painless lump on side of neck

pathognomonic.symptomName: External sinus or fistula opening along anterior border of sternocleidomastoid
searchTerms: skin opening or hole near neck muscle

common.symptomName: Intermittent swelling of the lateral neck mass
searchTerms: neck lump swelling on and off

common.symptomName: Recurrent neck infections or abscess formation at cyst site
Discharge from sinus or fistula tract
searchTerms: pus or fluid leaking from neck fistula
difficulty swallowing due to neck mass

occasional.symptomName: Limited neck range of motion secondary to swelling
searchTerms: difficulty moving neck due to swelling

rare.symptomName: Airway obstruction from large cystic mass
searchTerms: blocked airway from large neck cyst
breathing difficulty due to neck mass

rare.symptomName: Malignant transformation (rare squamous cell carcinoma arising in cyst)
Facial nerve palsy due to local inflammation or surgery
searchTerms: drooping face due to nerve damage

laboratory: Elevated inflammatory markers during infection (e.g., ESR, CRP)
Normal routine blood counts unless infected
imaging: Ultrasound showing well-defined anechoic cystic lesion
CT scan demonstrating cystic mass anterior to sternocleidomastoid with possible fistulous tract
MRI delineating cyst wall and relation to adjacent structures
genetic: No known genetic mutations associated; sporadic developmental anomaly
other: Histopathology showing cyst lined by stratified squamous or respiratory epithelium with lymphoid aggregates
Presence of fistulous tract connecting skin to pharynx in some cases

distinguishingFeatures: Moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion
Diffuse involvement of neck and sometimes axilla

redFlags: Rapid increase in size of neck mass
Persistent or recurrent infection despite treatment
Neurological deficits such as facial nerve palsy
references: James A. et al. Branchial cleft anomalies: diagnosis and management. Otolaryngol Clin North Am. 2020.
